environment.note: This is a compiler behavior + symbol-presence check, not a timing benchmark. The verdicts are deterministic: fixed sources + a pinned compiler produce fixed pass/fail and fixed stdout byte counts. CPU/GPU/RAM do not affect the result, so they are intentionally omitted.

subject.name: zig
subject.install: download zig-x86_64-windows-0.16.0.zip from https://ziglang.org/download/0.16.0/ and put zig on PATH
subject.note: Windows x86_64 baseline (Threaded I/O backend). The received binary zig-x86_64-windows-0.16.0.zip (97,217,739 bytes) was deleted after the run per firsthand cleanup policy.

baseline.name: zig 0.15 std.io idioms
baseline.note: Compared conceptually in the post (old std.io.getStdOut() / std.Thread.Pool vs the new std.Io interface). The 0.15 idioms are exercised here only as they FAIL to compile under 0.16 — the removal is the observation, not a timing comparison.

cross_platform.linux_io_uring: NOT measured. The evented io_uring backend (Linux) and its performance/behavior are cited from the release notes, explicitly flagged as not-firsthand.
cross_platform.macos_gcd: NOT measured. The evented GCD backend (macOS) is cited, not measured. All four probes here ran on the Windows x86_64 Threaded backend only.

raw_artifacts.retention_policy: none discarded — all evidence for this run is small and committed
raw_artifacts.note: The four .zig sources, probe.sh, and the deterministic probe-result.json are committed. No large raw artifacts exist. The 97 MB pinned zig toolchain was received, executed, and deleted (firsthand cleanup); run.sh re-fetches the same pinned version to reproduce.
